problem:
Meridian Bank receives a daily remittance file from Northgate Retail, a large corporate customer that pays several thousand suppliers in one batch. On a typical morning, around 90 percent of the transactions in the file enter the manual repair queue because key data is missing or inconsistent: beneficiary account numbers that fail the modulus check, remittance information that exceeds the permitted length, missing beneficiary names, and currency codes that do not match the beneficiary account currency. The repair team of six operators can clear roughly 400 items a day, while the file routinely contains more than 3,000 defective items, so the queue grows every day and the oldest items age past the customer's value-date promise.

The business impact is visible on three fronts at once. Suppliers complain to Northgate Retail about late payment, and Northgate Retail escalates to its relationship manager at Meridian Bank, threatening to move the business to a competitor. Operations management sees overtime rising and error rates climbing as operators rush, and two recent rushed repairs changed a beneficiary account number and sent funds to the wrong supplier, which then had to be recovered through a return process. Finance cannot close the daily reconciliation cleanly because repaired items lose their original references, so the same payment appears under two different identifiers in different reports.

The root tension is that the repair workbench is flexible enough to fix almost anything, which hides the real problem. Every defect that an operator can repair is a defect that the sending customer and the bank's own intake validation allowed through. The bank must decide how much repair flexibility to keep, which defects to prevent at source, and how to protect straight-through processing, customer experience and reconciliation while the file quality improves.
solution:
Start by measuring the problem properly. Classify every repair in the last four weeks by defect type, by source system and by field, and build a Pareto view so the team can see which five or six defect classes drive most of the 90 percent. For each class, decide whether it is preventable at intake, enrichable from reference data, or genuinely repairable only by a human. Typical preventable classes are account-number format failures, missing beneficiary names and remittance text over the permitted length, all of which can be validated in the customer upload portal with a clear, field-level error message that tells Northgate Retail exactly what to fix.

Second, redesign the repair workbench around control, not just speed. Repaired items must keep their original instruction reference and a full before-and-after audit record, so reconciliation can always trace a payment back to the file line it came from. Sensitive changes, above all beneficiary account numbers, require maker-checker approval and trigger re-validation and re-screening before release. The workbench should show the operator the permitted repair for each defect class, not a free-text edit of any field, and it should prioritise by value date and SLA so the items closest to breaching their promise are worked first.

Third, agree a staged improvement plan with the customer and with Operations. Publish a weekly defect report to Northgate Retail showing defect counts by class and the exact upload changes needed, and agree a target straight-through-processing rate with milestones rather than demanding perfection in one step. Internally, track straight-through-processing rate, repair ageing, rework rate and operator productivity daily, and review them in a short weekly forum with Operations, Product and the relationship manager. The goal is a file that mostly flows straight through, a small repair queue that is worked within SLA, and a full audit trail on every item that is touched.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Meridian Bank's payment operations team. The Northgate Retail remittance file has a 90 percent repair rate, the repair queue is growing daily, and two recent repairs sent funds to the wrong beneficiary. Senior management asks you to recommend the first intervention.

options.label: A
options.detail: Reject the entire file every day until Northgate Retail sends a perfect file, and hold all supplier payments until then.

options.label: B
options.detail: Segment defects by root cause and source, block the preventable defect classes at intake with actionable guidance to the customer, and prioritise the remaining repair queue by SLA and value date.

options.label: C
options.detail: Double the repair team and extend overtime so the queue clears each day, keeping the current repair workbench unchanged.

options.label: D
options.detail: Allow operators to repair any field without approval so items move faster, and reconcile the file only at month end.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because it attacks the root causes, stops preventable defects at source, and protects the queue that remains with SLA-based prioritisation. Option C only adds capacity to a broken process and leaves the error rate and wrong-beneficiary risk untouched. Option D removes controls and increases the risk of misdirected payments and lost traceability. Option A punishes the customer and all suppliers for defects that are partly the bank's own validation gap, and it breaks the value-date promise for every payment including the clean ones.

steps.title: Uploads the daily remittance file through the corporate upload portal
Validates file structure, account formats, currency and remittance length, and returns field-level errors for preventable defects
Enriches valid items from reference data, for example beneficiary name from the account directory where permitted
Routes clean items straight through and repairable items to the controlled repair workbench
Corrects only permitted fields, with maker-checker approval for beneficiary account changes
Re-validates and re-screens every repaired item before release
Executes the payment and generates the interbank message
Reconciles executed items against the original file lines using the preserved instruction reference

happy: Northgate Retail uploads a file that passes intake validation, with only a small number of genuinely repairable items. Clean items flow straight through to the payment engine and execute on the promised value date. Repairable items enter the workbench, are corrected within SLA with maker-checker approval where required, are re-validated and re-screened, and then execute. Every item reconciles to its original file line, the straight-through-processing rate is reported daily, and suppliers are paid on time.

negative.title: Repeated defect from the same source
negative.detail: The same account-format defect appears in every daily file because the customer's source system generates it. Flag the defect class in the Pareto report, raise it with the customer as a source-system fix, and add a targeted intake rule so the file is rejected with a precise message instead of entering repair each day.

negative.title: Repair changes the payment meaning
negative.detail: An operator corrects a beneficiary account number or amount and the payment no longer matches the customer's intent. Require maker-checker approval for sensitive fields, re-run validation and screening, and keep a before-and-after audit record; if the change is material and cannot be confirmed, return the item to the customer instead of releasing it.

negative.title: Repair queue exceeds SLA
negative.detail: Defect volume spikes and items age past their value date. Prioritise by value date and SLA, escalate to Operations management, notify the customer of the affected items and revised timing, and do not release items by skipping validation to catch up.

negative.title: Duplicate after resubmission
negative.detail: The customer resubmits a corrected file containing items that were already repaired and executed. Detect duplicates by instruction reference and idempotency key at intake, reject the duplicate lines with a clear reason, and reconcile the file against already-executed items before any new execution.

technical: Keep the original instruction reference immutable from intake to ledger so a repaired item never loses traceability. Use an idempotency key per file line so a resubmitted file cannot execute the same payment twice. Store every repair as a before-and-after event with operator, checker, timestamp, reason code and field-level change, retained for audit. Define editable fields by payment state, so a field that is editable in repair is locked once the item is released to the engine. Re-run sanctions and fraud screening after any material change to beneficiary, amount or currency. Capture defect codes in a governed catalogue with effective dates, and measure straight-through-processing rate, repair ageing, rework and operator productivity from the same event store so the metrics cannot drift from the underlying data.

accounting: Each executed item produces a debit to the Northgate Retail account and a corresponding interbank settlement entry, with the batch control total reconciled against the sum of executed items plus rejected and repaired items still in the queue. Repaired items must not create a second accounting event for the same instruction, so the ledger posts once per executed item, keyed to the original instruction reference. Items that cannot be repaired are rejected without a ledger posting, and the customer statement shows only executed payments. Operations works from a repair ageing worklist with SLA targets per value date, and any item that ages past its value date is escalated to the relationship manager and reported to the customer with a revised timing. Wrong-beneficiary repairs are treated as operational incidents with a recovery workflow and a root-cause review.

questions.explanation: The original reference is the link between the file line, the repair, the executed payment and the ledger. Without it, reconciliation cannot prove which file line produced which payment.
options: So reconciliation can trace the executed payment back to the original file line
So the repair operator can find it faster
So the payment engine can skip screening
So the customer can change the amount later

questions.explanation: Changing the beneficiary account redirects funds to a different account, so it carries the highest misdirection risk and needs a second person to check it.
options: Adding an internal note
Changing the beneficiary account number
Correcting a spelling error in remittance text
Reassigning the item to another operator

questions.explanation: Straight-through processing is the proportion of items that complete automatically. A low rate, such as 10 percent here, signals an intake or data quality problem, not just a staffing problem.

The size of the repair team
The share of items that flow from intake to execution without manual repair
How fast operators type
